prompt: Which design patterns does the .NET framework use?
completion:
Below is a “cheat‑sheet” of the most common **design patterns** that are baked into the .NET Framework (Core, 5/6/7/8 …) and some of the places where you’ll see them in the BCL, WPF, ASP.NET, Entity Framework, etc.  
(You can use this as a quick reference when you’re looking for a pattern or when you’re writing your own code that follows the same conventions.)

| Pattern | What it is | Where you’ll spot it in .NET |
|--------|------------|-----------------------------|
| **Singleton** | One instance, global access | `System.Configuration.ConfigurationManager`, `System.AppDomain`, `System.Diagnostics.Process`, `System.Environment`, `System.Collections.Concurrent.ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue>` (internally holds a singleton for caching), `Lazy<T>` |
| **Factory** | Creates objects, hides details | `Activator.CreateInstance`, `XmlReader.Create`, `StreamFactory` in `System.IO`, `DbProviderFactories.GetFactory`, `WebRequest.Create`, `Entity Framework DbContextOptionsBuilder`, `IServiceProvider.GetService` |
| **Builder** | Incrementally construct a complex object | `StringBuilder`, `UriBuilder`, `WebRequest.CreateBuilder`, `HttpClientBuilder` (ASP.NET Core) |
| **Prototype (Cloneable)** | Clone existing objects | `ICloneable`, `MemberwiseClone` (used internally by `MemberInfo`, `Assembly`), `Component` base class in WinForms/WPF |
| **Adapter** | Translate one interface to another | `ArrayList` to `IList<T>`, `System.IO.FileStream` adapter for `Stream`, `System.IO.TextReader` adapter for `StreamReader`, `IEnumerable` ↔ `IEnumerable<T>` via `Cast<T>()` |
| **Bridge** | Separate abstraction from implementation | `Graphics` (abstract) and `Graphics2D`/`GraphicsDevice` (concrete), `IAsyncResult`/`Task` |
| **Composite** | Treat individual and composites uniformly | `System.IO.FileSystemInfo` → `DirectoryInfo`/`FileInfo`; `System.Windows.Documents.Block`/`Inline` in WPF |
| **Decorator** | Wrap behavior dynamically | Stream wrappers (`BufferedStream`, `GZipStream`, `CryptoStream`), `TextReader`/`TextWriter` wrappers (`StreamReader`, `StreamWriter`, `BufferedStream`), `HttpClientHandler` chain |
| **Facade** | Simplify a complex subsystem | `System.IO.File`, `System.IO.Directory`, `System.IO.Path`, `System.Net.WebClient`, `System.Net.Http.HttpClient` |
| **Flyweight** | Share common state to reduce memory | `System.Text.StringBuilder` interned strings, `System.Drawing.Color`, `CultureInfo` (cached) |
| **Proxy** | Control access to another object | `TransparentProxy` (Remoting), `RealProxy`, `Lazy<T>` proxy, `LazyInitializer.EnsureInitialized` |
| **Chain of Responsibility** | Pass request along a chain | ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline, `HttpMessageHandler` chain, `DelegatingHandler` |
| **Command** | Encapsulate a request | `System.Windows.Input.ICommand`, `IAsyncCommand` (in MVVM libs), `SendOrPostCallback` |
| **Interpreter** | Evaluate language expressions | `System.Data.SqlClient.SqlCommand`, `Entity Framework LINQ expression trees` |
| **Iterator** | Traverse collection without exposing internals | `IEnumerable<T>`, `IEnumerator<T>`, `yield return` |
| **Mediator** | Reduce coupling by using a central hub | `IServiceProvider`/`IServiceCollection`, `EventAggregator` in Prism, `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` |
| **Memento** | Capture and restore state | `Undo/Redo` pattern in applications, `ICustomFormatter`/`IFormatProvider` (stateful) |
| **Observer** | Notify dependents of changes | .NET events (`EventHandler`, `EventHandler<T>`), `INotifyPropertyChanged`, `INotifyCollectionChanged`, `Reactive Extensions (Rx)` |
| **State** | Change behavior based on state | `TcpState` in `System.Net.Sockets`, `FileSystemWatcher.State` (internal), `Windows.Media.MediaState` |
| **Strategy** | Pick an algorithm at runtime | `IComparer<T>`, `IEqualityComparer<T>`, `XmlReaderSettings` strategies (`DtdProcessing`, `ValidationType`) |
| **Template Method** | Skeleton of an algorithm | `File.OpenRead`, `File.OpenWrite` (calls internal `FileStream` creation), `FileSystemWatcher` template for raising events |
| **Visitor** | Operate on elements of an object structure | LINQ expression tree visitors (`ExpressionVisitor`), `System.Xml.Linq.XObjectVisitor` |

---

### How the Patterns Show Up in .NET Architecture

| .NET Subsystem | Patterns Involved | Quick Note |
|----------------|-------------------|------------|
| **Base Class Library (BCL)** | All of the above (see table) | The BCL is a rich tapestry of patterns. |
| **WPF & WinForms** | Observer (events), Command (ICommand), Decorator (UIElements), Adapter (XAML ↔ code‑behind) | `INotifyPropertyChanged` + data binding = Observer. |
| **ASP.NET MVC / Web API** | MVC (Model‑View‑Controller), Strategy (routing), Factory (dependency injection), Observer (signals), Template Method (Controller actions) | The framework uses its own MVC pattern. |
| **Entity Framework** | Repository (DbSet<T>), Unit of Work (DbContext), Builder (Fluent API), Strategy (query execution), Visitor (expression tree parsing) | EF Core heavily relies on the Builder and Visitor patterns. |
| **WCF / gRPC** | Service Oriented Architecture (SOA) = Facade, Adapter (protocol adapters), Decorator (message inspectors), Factory (channel factories) | The WCF service stack uses many of the structural patterns. |
| **Razor Pages** | MVC, Observer (ChangeTracking), Template Method (page lifecycle), Strategy (route handling) | Razor Pages extends the MVC pattern. |
| **Dependency Injection** | Singleton, Factory, Strategy (service lifetime), Facade (IServiceProvider) | `IServiceCollection` and `IServiceProvider` are a textbook use of several patterns. |
| **Reactive Extensions (Rx)** | Observer, Iterator, Strategy (schedulers), Visitor (operators) | Rx is a prime example of the Observer pattern in action. |
| **LINQ** | Iterator, Visitor, Strategy (query provider), Builder (expression tree building) | `IQueryable<T>` and `ExpressionVisitor` are the core of LINQ. |

---

### Quick Checklist for Your Own Code

| Pattern | When to use it? | Example in .NET |
|---------|-----------------|-----------------|
| Singleton | Global shared resource (e.g., logging, config) | `ILoggerFactory` |
| Factory | You need to create different subclasses based on input | `DbConnectionFactory` |
| Builder | You have a lot of optional settings | `StringBuilder`, `UriBuilder` |
| Observer | One object needs to notify many others | Events (`EventHandler`), `INotifyPropertyChanged` |
| Strategy | Different algorithms for the same task | `IComparer<T>` |
| Decorator | Add behavior to an object without subclassing | `Stream` wrappers |
| Facade | Simplify a complex subsystem | `System.IO.File` static class |

---

### References

* **Microsoft Docs – Design Patterns**  
  https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-patterns/  
  (Shows how .NET uses each pattern)

* **.NET Framework Design Guidelines**  
  https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/  

* **C# Design Patterns by James Newkirk**  
  (Good book that maps .NET classes to patterns)

---

**Bottom line:**  
The .NET Framework itself is a living example of well‑architected design‑pattern use. Whether you’re using a simple `StringBuilder`, wiring up a WPF data‑binding pipeline, or building a high‑performance ASP.NET Core application, you’re already interacting with a collection of patterns that were chosen by the framework designers for robustness, extensibility, and testability. Use the table above as a reference to spot the patterns in your own code and to decide which one fits the problem you’re trying to solve.
